analysis.one_liner: Lets workers unionize by signing cards instead of a company-run election, with binding first-contract arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, vote, or even a single cosponsor before the session ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so that when a majority of workers at a workplace signs cards saying they want a union, the government certifies the union directly — skipping the secret-balllot election employers currently control the timing of. It would then force the company to start bargaining within 10 days, bring in a federal mediator if talks stall after 90 days, and impose a binding two-year contract through arbitration if mediation fails. It would also speed up government handling of complaints that a company illegally punished union supporters and add triple back pay plus fines up to $20,000 per violation for employers caught doing it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize a union at their workplace. Card-sign certification removes the period between announcing a union drive and the election — when employers can legally hold captive-audience meetings and often fire organizers and pay only back pay later. Faster first contracts and arbitration stop companies from bargaining in bad faith for years. Penalties raise the price of firing union supporters.

how_it_helps.text: Once a majority of workers signs valid authorization cards, the NLRB must certify the union without an election, eliminating the employer-controlled waiting period where workers are most vulnerable to pressure [S2] [S3].

Employers would have to begin bargaining within 10 days, and if 90 days of talks plus 30 days of mediation fail, a binding arbitration contract takes effect for two years — ending the common strategy of refusing to agree to any first contract [S2] [S3].

Complaints that an employer fired or threatened union supporters during an organizing drive would get priority investigation, and the worker would recover triple back pay; willful or repeated violators face fines up to $20,000 per violation [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing organizing drives, who would lose the ability to delay certification through the election process, stall first contracts indefinitely, and fire union supporters with only delayed back pay as the penalty. Employers found to have violated the law during organizing would pay substantially more.

drawbacks.text: Replacing secret-ballot elections with card signing means workers would sign authorizations under whatever pressure union organizers apply — the same criticism made of the original 2009 Employee Free Choice Act. Supporters counter that workers already face employer pressure during elections.

Binding first-contract arbitration lets an outside panel set wages, benefits, and work rules for two years without either side agreeing, which employers argue substitutes a government-imposed contract for negotiated one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shifted real power from employers to workers seeking representation: faster certification, faster contracts, and penalties that make firing organizers costly. The trade-offs — union pressure during card signing and arbitrator-set contracts — are the price of that shift, and the bill gives workers the stronger hand by design. As written it was also a heavy lift: a single sponsor with no cosponsors and no committee movement gave it no realistic path.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Education and the Workforce Committee and later to a subcommittee, and nobody ever scheduled a hearing or vote before the session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the bill on April 20, 2016, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1] [S5].

In September 2016 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers opposing union organizing are better off, since the current system — employer-timed elections, no penalty for refusing a first contract, and back-pay-only remedies for firing organizers — remains in place. The bill died without a hearing, so no one else gained anything from it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat, drew no cosponsors from either party, and sat in a Republican-controlled committee with a Republican majority, so it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would remove the election-delay tactic, force binding first contracts, and attach real fines and triple back pay to firing or threatening union supporters. Its costs fall on companies that benefit from workers staying unorganized.
Unions would gain members through card-sign certification and enforceable first contracts. The bill's benefits to workers organizing runs through and alongside union growth.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and management-side labor law firms
industries.note: A large consulting industry exists to run employer campaigns against organizing drives; card-sign certification and steeper penalties for retaliation would sharply cut demand for those services.
